# donchian_breakout / 1

**Hypothesis.** A close above the highest high of the last 20 days marks the start of a volatility expansion in
the direction of the break, and such moves tend to run (the classic channel breakout of trend followers).

**Rule.** Upper channel = highest high of the previous 480 bars, lower channel = lowest low of the previous 240
bars (both exclude the current bar). A symbol is held (`1/N`) if, inside the lookback window, its most recent
channel event is a close above the upper channel rather than a close below the lower one; otherwise USDC.
The position state is rebuilt from the window at every call (the function keeps no memory), so the lookback
(2 200 bars) must be several times the channel length; with no event in the window the symbol is not held.

**What would refute it.** False breakouts: the price closes above the channel and falls back, and the exit only
comes at the 10-day low, far below the entry. Few trades, so the estimate of any edge is noisy.

# garch_regime / 1

**Hypothesis.** Volatility clusters and is forecastable; the days that follow a high conditional-volatility
forecast carry more downside than upside for a long-only holder. Staying out of the market when a GARCH(1,1)
model announces a turbulent day, and following the daily trend otherwise, should cut drawdowns more than returns.

**Rule.** Hourly bars are reduced to the last close of each complete UTC day (180 days of lookback). For each
symbol: (1) trend: last daily close above the mean of the last 30 daily closes; (2) regime: fit a zero-mean
GARCH(1,1) (`arch`) on the daily log-returns of the window and compare the one-day-ahead volatility forecast with
the median fitted volatility of the window; the regime is calm if `forecast <= 1.25 x median`. Weight `1/N` when
both hold, otherwise USDC. If the optimiser does not converge the symbol is not held.

**Cadence.** The output only changes when a UTC day completes, and a fit costs tens of milliseconds, so the
backtests of this strategy use `--decision-every 24` (one decision per day, at 00:00 UTC). The live engine should
call it at the same cadence.

**What would refute it.** GARCH forecasts react AFTER a large move (the shock enters the variance with a lag of one
day), so the filter may step aside after the fall and miss the rebound. About 180 daily observations is a short
sample for a GARCH fit: the parameters are noisy and the threshold `1.25` is arbitrary.

# ma_trend / 1

**Hypothesis.** Trends persist: when the average price of the last 3 days is above the average of the last 20 days,
the asset is in an up-trend that is more likely to continue than to stop, and being out of the market otherwise
avoids the large drawdowns of a long-only holder.

**Rule.** For each symbol: weight `1/N` if `mean(close[-72:]) > mean(close[-480:])`, otherwise 0 (USDC).

**What would refute it.** Whipsaws: in a range-bound market the two averages cross often and every crossing costs
fee + slippage on the whole position. The rule is always late (it enters after the rise began and leaves after
the fall began); if trends are short relative to the 20-day window it loses to buy-and-hold.

# mean_reversion / 1

**Hypothesis.** Over a couple of days, a sharp move away from the recent average price is partly a liquidity shock
that reverts: an asset trading well below its 48-hour mean tends to bounce back towards it (the lower Bollinger
band as a buy zone).

**Rule.** `z = (close - mean48) / std48`. Weight per symbol = `(1/N) * clip(-z / z_full, 0, 1)`: nothing at or above
the mean, scaling in linearly below it, fully in at `z <= -2`. There is no memory: the position shrinks as the
price returns to its mean. Long-only, so it never sells the upper band short.

**What would refute it.** It buys falling prices: in a sustained down-trend it is repeatedly long while the price
keeps falling ("catching a falling knife"). It trades often, so costs weigh heavily; with 20 bps per side the
average bounce must be several times larger than that to leave anything.

# pairs_rotation / 1

**Hypothesis.** Some pairs of crypto assets share a common stochastic trend (they are cointegrated over windows of
a few weeks): the residual of a regression of one log-price on the other is stationary, so when it is far from zero
the "cheap" leg should outperform the "expensive" one as the spread closes.

**Rule.** Pairs: ETH/BTC and SOL/LINK, half of the portfolio each. On the last 720 bars, regress `log A` on `log B`
(OLS with intercept), take the z-score of the last residual and the Dickey-Fuller t-statistic of the residuals
(no lags). If the t-statistic is below -3.34 (Engle-Granger 5 % critical value for two series) and `z < -1`, the
pair's budget goes entirely to A; if `z > 1`, entirely to B; otherwise it is split equally between the two legs.

**This is not a market-neutral pairs trade.** A wallet that cannot short cannot isolate the spread: the strategy is
always fully invested and carries the whole market risk. All it can do is tilt between two assets it would hold
anyway; its fair comparison is the equal-weight benchmark, and the most it can add is the spread convergence.

**What would refute it.** The cointegration test is repeated every hour on a rolling window (a multiple-testing
problem in itself) and rolling-window cointegration between crypto assets is unstable: a "cheap" leg can simply be
the one that is losing for a durable reason. Each rotation costs fee + slippage on half the portfolio, twice.

# ts_momentum / 1

**Hypothesis.** Returns of liquid crypto assets are positively autocorrelated at the horizon of a few weeks: an asset
that went up over the last 30 days is more likely to keep going up than to reverse (time-series momentum, Moskowitz,
Ooi & Pedersen 2012).

**Rule.** For each symbol: weight `1/N` if `close[t] > close[t - window]` (window = 720 hourly bars = 30 days),
otherwise 0. The unused part stays in USDC.

**What would refute it.** No improvement over buy-and-hold in drawdown or Sharpe ratio after costs, out of sample.
The signal flips when the price crosses its level of 30 days ago, which can cause repeated in-and-out trades in a
flat market; each flip costs fee + slippage on the whole position.

# vol_target_trend / 1

**Hypothesis.** Volatility is persistent and high volatility is not rewarded with proportionally higher returns, so
sizing a trend position inversely to recent realised volatility gives a smoother ride (smaller drawdowns for a
similar return) than a fixed-size trend position.

**Rule.** Same trend signal as `ma_trend/1` (72-bar mean above 480-bar mean). When it is on, the weight is
`(1/N) * min(1, target_vol / realised_vol)`, with `realised_vol` the annualised standard deviation of the last 168
hourly log-returns and `target_vol` = 40 % per year. There is no leverage: the weight is capped at `1/N`, so the
strategy can only reduce risk, never add to it.

**What would refute it.** If volatility spikes mostly AFTER the losses, scaling down comes too late and only
removes exposure to the rebound. The weight moves a little every hour; without a rebalance threshold this
generates many small trades and costs.

# xs_momentum / 1

**Hypothesis.** Relative strength persists: among the assets of the universe, those with the best return over the
last 30 days keep outperforming the others over the following days (cross-sectional momentum, Jegadeesh & Titman
1993, here on a handful of crypto assets).

**Rule.** Rank the symbols by `close[t] / close[t - 720] - 1` and hold the best `top_k` = 2 with equal weights.
The strategy is ALWAYS fully invested: it selects among assets, it does not time the market, so it carries the
full market risk of a long-only crypto holder. Its fair comparison is the equal-weight benchmark.

**What would refute it.** With four highly correlated assets the cross-section is tiny: rank changes are mostly
noise, each change costs fee + slippage on half the portfolio, and the result can be dominated by one asset.

# xs_momentum / 3

Universe-generic version: `META["universe"] = ["*"]`. The symbols are not written in the strategy; they are the ones the
agent trades (1 to 12 market symbols, at least 3 here), passed by the engine with the candles and by `--symbols` to the backtest.
Same rule and same parameters as version 1: nothing was re-tuned, for any universe. A ranking needs something to rank: with fewer than 3 symbols the function returns cash, `META["min_symbols"] = 3` makes the signal runner refuse the input, and the API refuses to register this version for such an agent. `top_k = 2` is carried over from version 1: with 3 symbols the strategy holds the best two.

SPW_RESEARCH_RUNNER_SECRET is not set: the runner routes answer 404, research jobs stay queued
